instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "Do LSTM / deep hydrologic models beat gradient-boosted trees for ungauged basins at small n"

### Research question
In head-to-head, SPATIALLY HELD-OUT comparisons, do LSTM, entity-aware LSTM, or hybrid differentiable models beat gradient-boosted decision trees for ungauged-basin prediction, specifically for WATER QUALITY targets? And at what number of training basins does any deep-model advantage actually appear?

### What a good answer contains
The specific PUB experiments (Kratzert et al. 2019 "Towards learning universal, regional and local hydrological behaviors via machine learning"; Kratzert et al. ungauged-basin work) with their metrics AND basin counts. Any ablation reporting performance vs NUMBER OF TRAINING BASINS. Any study applying LSTM to nitrate or nutrient CONCENTRATION with spatial holdout - and whether it beat RF/XGBoost or merely beat a linear baseline. An explicit note on whether reported gains persist under leave-one-REGION-out rather than leave-one-basin-out. A recommendation on the cheaper middle ground: multi-task / shared-embedding models, site-embedding regularization, or per-site random effects layered on top of the existing booster.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].

tier1_survived.claim: Pandit et al. (2025, WRR 61(8), doi:10.1029/2024WR039207) trained an LSTM on daily stream nitrate across the conterminous US and reported a large drop from temporal to spatial validation: median KGE fell from 0.60 (temporal validation, forecasting unseen periods at sites INCLUDED in training) to 0.18 (spatial validation, prediction at basins NOT in training). This is the closest published analogue to our deployment target and says an LSTM does not solve the ungauged-basin nitrate-concentration problem.
tier1_survived.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal) -> 0.18 (spatial holdout); a drop of 0.42 KGE
tier1_survived.nBasins: 95 sites used for model training/validation (drawn from 148 total monitoring locations, 1980-2022)
corrections:
The claim is directionally correct and its two quoted numbers are exact, but it should be restated as follows before use.

Pandit et al. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," WRR 61(8), e2024WR039207, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207 (CC-BY-NC), trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate CONCENTRATION. Under temporal validation (unseen periods at sites included in training) median KGE = 0.60. Under spatial validation, which the authors define as "prediction in unmonitored basins," median KGE = 0.18 across all CONUS sites — BUT median KGE = 0.34 when restricted to the Mississippi River Basin, which the authors report as the reason they considered the model fit for MRB application.

Use the 0.34 figure, not 0.18, when reasoning about Iowa: Iowa is in the MRB and is named explicitly in the paper's abstract. The region-matched degradation is 0.60 -> 0.34 (drop 0.26), not 0.60 -> 0.18 (drop 0.42). Citing 0.18 for an Iowa-facing argument overstates the collapse by roughly 60%.

Three further fixes: (1) the "1980-2022" span is the MRB hindcast/application period, not the LSTM training period, and must not be described as the training window; (2) the "95 of 148 sites" counts are unverified — the full text is behind Cloudflare at Wiley and the PMC copy is embargoed until 2026-08-09 — so cite them only with that caveat, or re-check after that date; (3) KGE on a concentration time series is not comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 on a binary exceedance target, so this paper cannot be used to say our numbers beat or trail theirs.

The claim's core inference survives all of this and in fact strengthens: an LSTM does NOT solve ungauged-basin nitrate concentration, and it fails in the same way we do — timing preserved, absolute level lost. Given that the study likely had 5-8x more independent spatial units than our 19 basin families, an LSTM at our sample size should be expected to underperform the current XGBoost, not rescue it. The paper's more useful contribution to this project is not the pessimistic benchmark but its Shapley finding that tile drainage is the leading spatial control on mean nitrate concentration, which independently confirms the project's own between-site diagnosis and points at the missing feature.

The claim is accurate on every quoted figure but omits a qualifier the abstract itself supplies, and that qualifier is the one that applies to us.

1. MRB-specific number omitted. The abstract's next sentence reports spatial-validation median KGE = 0.34 within the Mississippi River Basin, versus 0.18 CONUS-wide. Iowa sits inside the MRB. The correct effect size for our domain is a drop of 0.60 -> 0.34 (0.26 KGE), not 0.60 -> 0.18 (0.42 KGE). The claim's headline drop is roughly 60% larger than the regionally applicable one. The conclusion survives — KGE 0.34 is still weak, and "an LSTM does not solve the ungauged-basin nitrate problem" stands — but the magnitude as stated is not the number to cite for an Iowa product. Cite 0.34, and note 0.18 as the CONUS-wide figure. The authors' own framing is that the CONUS/MRB gap is the point: spatial validation was used to identify data gaps and to justify restricting application to the region where transfer was better.

2. n = "95 sites drawn from 148 monitoring locations" is UNVERIFIED, not confirmed. Do not present it as sourced. Full text was unreachable (Wiley Cloudflare/402; PMC embargoed until 2026-08-09, one day after this check; no repository preprint; search budget exhausted). Re-verify after 2026-08-09 via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12425153/, which will then be free full text. Confirmed from the abstract: 1980-2022 is the MRB application period.

3. Temporal-validation definition is the claim's gloss, not the paper's words. "Forecasting unseen periods at sites included in training" is the standard meaning and is almost certainly right, but it is not verbatim from any accessible text. The spatial-validation gloss IS the authors' own ("prediction in unmonitored basins").

4. Add the tile-drainage finding when using this source. Shapley analysis in this paper ranks tile drainage among the top spatial drivers of mean nitrate concentration — independent support for our identified missing feature, and a lead worth following into the paper's data sources once full text is available.

5. Scope the conclusion. Because KGE and AUC/PR-AUC are not commensurable, this paper bounds the "would an LSTM fix our between-site problem?" question only. It says nothing about whether our XGBoost's AUC 0.820 is near a ceiling.

The claim is directionally correct and its quoted numbers are exact, but it must be corrected on three points before use.

(1) MATERIAL OMISSION — the 0.18 is the wrong stratum for Iowa. The paper reports a THIRD headline number the claim drops: spatial validation restricted to the Mississippi River Basin gave median KGE = 0.34, roughly double the CONUS-wide 0.18. The 0.18 is depressed by arid/mountainous regions with almost no nitrate sensors. Iowa is in the core MRB, so 0.34 is the figure describing ungauged-basin transfer in our domain. Cite as "median KGE fell from 0.60 (temporal) to 0.18 (spatial, CONUS-wide) and 0.34 (spatial, within the Mississippi River Basin)". The paper is therefore weaker evidence for pessimism about Iowa ungauged transfer than the claim asserts — it actually shows transfer improves substantially when the training and target domains are hydrologically matched.

(2) DATE-RANGE MISATTRIBUTION. "1980-2022" is the MRB simulation/application period, NOT the training window. Training used high-frequency nitrate SENSOR data, which is essentially post-2010. The claim's metadata field conflates the two.

(3) UNVERIFIED n. "95 sites used for model training/validation (drawn from 148 total monitoring locations)" could not be substantiated from any accessible source (full text paywalled at Wiley, PMC embargoed to 2026-08-09). Report the site count as unverified rather than as fact, or defer citing an n until the PMC embargo lifts on 2026-08-09.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR THIS PROJECT: (a) KGE on a continuous daily concentration series is NOT comparable to our AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 on a binary exceedance target — there is no arithmetic bridge, so this paper cannot validate or indict our numbers, only the qualitative temporal-vs-spatial gap. (b) Their n (~95 sensor sites nationally, unverified) is the same order as our 85 sites but almost certainly exceeds our 19 independent basin families; the n=19 constraint remains more severe for us and this paper does not relieve it. (c) The paper's most actionable content for us is not the KGE drop but the Shapley result naming tile drainage, roadway density, and wetland cover as the dominant controls on MEAN (between-site) nitrate concentration — direct external confirmation that our between-site deficit is a missing-static-attribute problem, with tile drainage first on the list.

Its site-level performance was explicitly conditional on high-frequency SENSOR data density (EPA record: agricultural Midwest sites reached R2 and KGE > 0.7 while data-sparse western sites fell below 0.3), i.e. the reported skill is driven by data-rich sites rather than by architecture. Any inference that an LSTM would transfer at n=19 families is unsupported by this source.
tier1_survived.effectSize: median R2 and KGE ~0.5 across all sites; >0.7 in agricultural Midwest, <0.3 in data-sparse West
tier1_survived.nBasins: 148 monitoring locations total; 95 used for training/validation
corrections:
The claim is directionally correct and its conclusion stands, but three details need fixing before it is used.

(1) The cited source is NOT a paper. It is an EPA Science Inventory record for a PRESENTATION given at the AGU 2023 Fall Meeting (Pandit, Lane, Christensen, Golden & Husic, 2023), consisting of a single-paragraph abstract with no methods, no DOI, and no peer review. Say "conference abstract," not "the paper." This makes the source weaker evidence than the claim implies — it cannot support ANY methodological inference, favorable or unfavorable.

(2) The "95 sites used for training/validation" figure is not in the cited record; the string does not appear. The only site count given is 148 total, with no stated train/validation partition. Drop the "95-148" range and state "148 sites, partition not reported." The ratio to our 19 families is therefore ~7.8x, not "5-8x."

(3) Strengthen the operative objection. The decisive problem is not primarily the basin count — it is that the source's own explanatory claim is "the necessity of sensor data for accurate simulations," and it attributes the <0.3 western scores to sensor absence. Since our deployment target is an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin with no nitrate history, this source's stated mechanism predicts failure at the target regardless of n or architecture. The n=19 constraint is a second, independent objection, not the main one.

Additionally: because the record reports no split protocol, its R2/KGE values must not be placed on the same axis as our LOFO 0.820 / R2 0.328 under any circumstance. If the LSTM line of inquiry is to be pursued, it needs the peer-reviewed journal version of this work (which may contain the 95 figure and a stated protocol) or a source with an explicit ungauged-basin / leave-one-region-out protocol — not this abstract.

The claim is correct in substance and its quoted metrics are exact, but two details should be tightened before use:

(1) The "95 used for training/validation" figure is NOT in the cited EPA Science Inventory record — the number 95 does not appear there at all. Only 148 sites (1980-2022) is verifiable from this URL. Either drop "95-148" and say "148 monitoring sites, roughly 7.8x our 19 independent basin families," or attach a separate citation for the 95 figure.

(2) Calling it "the paper" overstates the artifact. It is an AGU 2023 Fall Meeting PRESENTATION record (Pandit, Lane, Christensen, Golden & Husic, presented 2023-12-15), with no abstract section, no methods, and no reported split protocol. This makes the claim STRONGER, not weaker: the objection is not merely "no basin-count ablation was reported" but "no evaluation protocol of any kind was reported," so the median R2/KGE ~0.5 cannot be placed on the same axis as our LOFO numbers under rule 1, and the source cannot support any inference about LSTM transfer — at n=19 or at any n.

The claim is correct in substance but has two factual errors of detail that should be fixed before it is used.

1. The "95 used for training/validation" figure is NOT in the cited source and should be dropped from any characterization of it. The EPA record states 148 sites and gives no training/validation breakdown. The 95 figure appears to be imported from a different (likely later, peer-reviewed) Pandit/Lane/Christensen/Golden/Husic publication and must not be attributed to this record. The defensible statement is: "its evidence base is 148 sites, with no reported train/validation partition." If the 95 number matters, it needs its own citation, which I could not obtain (web search budget for this session was exhausted after the primary-source fetch).

2. The source is not a "paper." It is an AGU 2023 Fall Meeting conference abstract / presentation record, not peer-reviewed, with no DOI. This strengthens rather than weakens the claim: faulting an abstract for "reporting no ablation" is trivially true because an abstract reports essentially no methodology at all. The sharper and more defensible framing is: this source is a conference abstract that reports no methods, no split protocol, and no ablations, and therefore cannot bear ANY inferential weight about architecture transfer at reduced n — the problem is not a missing ablation, it is that there is no methodological content to evaluate.

One addition worth carrying forward: the claim says the reported skill is "driven by data-rich sites rather than by architecture." That is the authors' own stated conclusion, not an adversarial reading — they write that they "highlight the necessity of sensor data for accurate simulations." Quoting them directly on this is stronger than paraphrasing it as an inference.

tier1_survived.claim: Kratzert et al. (2024, HESS 28:4187-4201) is a streamflow-only opinion paper: every experiment predicts daily volumetric DISCHARGE on the 531-basin CAMELS(-US) benchmark set. Full text contains NO water-quality, nutrient, or nitrate application, and NO comparison against gradient-boosted trees, XGBoost, or random forests — the only non-LSTM baselines are the conceptual model mHM and process-based model VIC. Therefore it provides ZERO direct evidence on whether LSTMs beat GBDTs for nitrate concentration in ungauged basins.
tier1_survived.effectSize: n/a — no GBDT and no water-quality experiment exists in the paper
corrections: The claim is accurate in every checkable particular (title/venue/pages, opinion-paper status, discharge-only target, 531 vs 489 basin counts, mHM and VIC as the only non-LSTM baselines, zero water-quality and zero GBDT content). Two refinements, both of which reinforce rather than weaken it: (1) The claim's "Reported split protocol: not-applicable" understates a material point — the paper's protocol is explicitly stated and is TEMPORAL-ONLY ("all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)"). There is no PUB/held-out-basin experiment anywhere in it, so the paper also provides zero direct evidence about ungauged-basin transfer, independent of the nitrate and GBDT gaps. (2) The model-type labels are slightly loose: mHM is a distributed (not purely conceptual) hydrologic model and VIC is a macroscale land-surface model; this does not affect the substance of the claim. The paper's one genuinely transferable takeaway is the pooling argument itself (train across basins, never on one), which our project already satisfies and which cannot deliver further gains at n=19 families.

Claim is accurate as stated; only additive precision is warranted. (i) Bibliographic detail: authors are Kratzert, Gauch, Klotz, and Nearing; the article type is literally "HESS Opinions" (a position paper), so "opinion paper" is exact, not a characterization. (ii) The claim lists the split protocol as "not-applicable"; more precisely, the experiments use GAUGED-basin temporal splits (train Oct 1999-Sep 2008, test Oct 1989-Sep 1999, "all models were tested on the same basins where they were trained (during different time periods)"). This makes the paper doubly non-comparable to the project's LOFO 0.820 — wrong target variable AND a level-memorization-permitting protocol. (iii) The terms "ungauged"/"prediction in ungauged basins" DO appear in the text, but only as motivating prose, never as an experiment; the authors explicitly state "this analysis does not account for the value of hydrologic diversity for prediction in ungauged basins." A careless reader searching for "ungauged" could wrongly conclude the paper contains PUB results, so the claim should be phrased as "no ungauged-basin EXPERIMENT" rather than implying the word is absent. (iv) Worth flagging for downstream use: the paper's Figs. 6-7 (performance vs. number/grouping of training basins, drawn from a 531-basin pool) are the only part relevant to this project, and they argue LSTMs need many basins — evidence against, not for, an LSTM at n=19 independent basin families.

The claim is correct on substance and on every quoted number; two refinements, neither of which changes its conclusion.

(1) "Reported split protocol: not-applicable" is the one imprecise field. The paper does have an explicit and consequential protocol: temporal holdout at the SAME basins the model was trained on. Main setup: "time periods for training (1 October 1999 through 30 September 2008), validation (1 October 1980 through 30 September 1989), and testing (1 October 1989 through 30 September 1999)." The Fig. 6 sample-size experiment uses "k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)." So it is a GAUGED-basin, temporally-split protocol — the weakest possible protocol relative to our LOFO. Under rule 1 none of its NSE numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, and this fact makes the claim's conclusion stronger, not weaker: the paper does not even measure spatial transfer, which is exactly the axis our project is stuck on. (Minor internal inconsistency worth noting: the Fig. 6 passage says training period "1999-2000" and test period "1980-1989", swapping the roles of the validation and test windows given in the main setup. Looks like an editing slip in the paper; immaterial here.)

(2) The paper contains one section that DOES bear on our situation, and it cuts against using this paper to justify anything at n=19 — worth surfacing rather than discarding. Section 4 "How many basins are necessary?" finds median NSE still rising monotonically at 531 basins: "even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow." Section 5 additionally trains on basins grouped by USGS HUC — "There are 18 HUCs represented in the CAMELS data set, with between 2 and 79 basins per HUC" — i.e. groupings of roughly the size of our 19 independent basin families, and the conclusion is that restricting to such groups is WORSE than pooling everything: "even if enough basins exist to divide your training data into hydrologically informed training sets, one is likely to be better off simply training a single model with all available data." So the paper's own evidence says an LSTM at our effective sample size sits far down the left tail of its learning curve. Anyone citing Kratzert et al. 2024 as support for switching this project from XGBoost to an LSTM is citing a paper that (a) never tested a GBDT, (b) never touched water quality, (c) never held out a basin spatially, and (d) whose sample-size analysis implies our n is well below where regional LSTMs start to pay off.

tier1_refuted.claim: In the same study, the temporal-to-spatial KGE degradation was strongly TARGET-DEPENDENT across all 95 CONUS sites: streamflow 0.78 -> 0.65 (drop 0.13), nitrate YIELD 0.59 -> 0.32 (drop 0.27), nitrate CONCENTRATION 0.60 -> 0.18 (drop 0.42). Concentration - our target - degrades ~3x more than discharge under spatial holdout, i.e. the between-site level of nitrate CONCENTRATION is the hardest quantity to transfer, even for a deep model with continental training data.
why:
SOURCE IDENTIFIED AND PARTIALLY ACCESSIBLE. The DOI resolves to: Pandit, Golden, Christensen, Lane & Husic (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8), e2024WR039207, CC-BY-NC. Wiley returns 403/402 to automated fetch; the PMC deposit (PMC12425153) is an EPA author manuscript still under EMBARGO, so only the abstract is retrievable (verified via Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and NCBI efetch — all four return the identical abstract text). Unpaywall lists no PDF at any location. Full text (Methods, results tables) could NOT be obtained.

WHAT THE ABSTRACT ACTUALLY SAYS, VERBATIM:
"We developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US to predict daily nitrate concentrations, achieving strong temporal validation performance (median KGE = 0.60). Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)."

ROW 1 OF THE CLAIM IS EXACT. Nitrate concentration 0.60 -> 0.18, drop 0.42, spatial-holdout / prediction-in-unmonitored-basins protocol: verbatim correct, correct protocol label, correct metric (median KGE across sites).

ROWS 2 AND 3 ARE UNSUBSTANTIATED. The abstract describes a single-target model — an LSTM "to predict daily nitrate concentrations." Nothing in any accessible text indicates that streamflow or nitrate yield were separately modeled and scored with KGE under both a temporal and a spatial protocol. The purported streamflow 0.78 -> 0.65 and nitrate yield 0.59 -> 0.32 pairs appear in no retrievable part of the record. Nitrate yield in this paper is a DERIVED quantity used for the mass-balance analysis (the "19 ± 4% of surplus" export fractions, Iowa wet-year 42 ± 24% vs dry-year 6 ± 6%), not a separately validated prediction target with its own KGE. tier1_refuted.claim: Restricting spatial validation to the Mississippi River Basin - a climatically and agriculturally homogeneous subregion containing Iowa - raised median spatial-holdout KGE for nitrate concentration from 0.18 (CONUS) to 0.34 (MRB). why:
SOURCE IS REAL AND THE NUMBERS ARE EXACT. DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207 = Pandit A., Golden H.E., Christensen J.R., Lane C.R., Husic A., "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8):e2024WR039207, published 2025-08-09, CC BY-NC. Publisher HTML/PDF returns HTTP 402/403; PMC copy (PMC12425153) is under NIH embargo until 2026-08-09 ("This article will be available in PMC on August 09, 2026"). I retrieved the full publisher abstract verbatim from the DOAJ API record (https://doaj.org/api/articles/1995df0df98e4f65bf55b0c621ba2e51), confirmed against Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, and Europe PMC.

Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)."

WHAT IS CORRECT: the three quoted numbers (0.60 temporal, 0.18 CONUS spatial, 0.34 MRB spatial) are exact and correctly attributed; the target is daily nitrate CONCENTRATION (not streamflow); the protocol is explicitly named "spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins," i.e. a PUB/spatial-holdout protocol, which is the protocol class comparable to our LOFO.

The claim's first sentence ("restricting spatial VALIDATION to the MRB raised median KGE 0.18 -> 0.34") is accurate. Its second sentence — that this is "direct evidence that transfer performance improves when the TRAINING POOL is restricted to hydroclimatically similar basins, supporting a regionally-specialized model over a continental one" — does not follow and is not supported by the source. The abstract describes ONE model ("a long short-term memory (LSTM) model using high-frequency sensor data from across the conterminous US") and then "the model's targeted application to the MRB" — definite article, singular, the same CONUS-trained model. The 0.34 is the MRB subset of the held-out folds of the CONUS-trained model, not a separately trained MRB-only model. Nothing in the abstract reports an ablation in which the training pool was varied (CONUS-trained vs MRB-trained, evaluated on the same MRB holdouts), which is the experiment the claim requires. The 0.18 -> 0.34 gap is equally or better explained by (a) MRB holdout basins being denser in, and more similar to, the CONUS training population (US high-frequency nitrate sensors are heavily Midwest-concentrated), and (b) MRB nitrate having higher variance and a stronger seasonal signal, which inflates KGE relative to low-signal western/eastern basins. Both are properties of the EVALUATION set, not of the training set.

THE PAPER'S ACTUAL DESIGN POINTS THE OPPOSITE WAY FOR US. The workflow is: train on the largest available pool (all CONUS sensors), then apply regionally. That is an argument for ENLARGING the training pool beyond Iowa while targeting Iowa at inference — precisely the lever that attacks our binding constraint of 19 independent basin families — not for staying Iowa-only. Used as stated, the claim would endorse the status quo and discourage the one intervention that could add independent between-site units.

METHODOLOGY / TRANSFERABILITY CAVEATS I COULD NOT RESOLVE (full text embargoed): (1) n basins is NOT verifiable from open metadata — the claim's own "95 training sites" is unsourced, and the MRB spatial-holdout subset count is unknown; a median KGE over an unknown and possibly single-digit number of held-out MRB basins is a fragile statistic. (2) The LSTM's input list is not in the abstract; LSTM nitrate-concentration models of this type commonly ingest DISCHARGE as a dynamic forcing. If so, the 0.34 is achieved at sites with streamflow information, which our deployment target (arbitrary map pin, no gauge, no local history) does not have — only 22 of our 85 sites have discharge and zero of the 61 IWQIS sites do. (3) Metric mismatch: KGE on a continuous daily concentration series is not comparable to our LOFO CLF AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634, and is not comparable to our REG LOFO R2 0.328 either (KGE and R2 are different functionals; KGE rewards matching mean and variance, which is exactly the between-site level term we fail at, so a KGE of 0.34 is if anything a WEAK ungauged-basin result). (4) The paper's own headline spatial numbers (0.18 CONUS, 0.34 MRB) confirm that state-of-the-art deep learning at continental scale still transfers poorly to unmonitored basins for nitrate concentration — consistent with, not superior to, our position.

INCIDENTAL BUT ACTIONABLE: the abstract's Shapley analysis names "tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover" as the top SPATIAL drivers of mean nitrate concentration across the MRB. That is independent support for the project's own diagnosis that the deficit is in between-site STATIC information, and it confirms a basin-wide tile-drainage layer exists and is usable at MRB extent — which is the feature our notes list as the dominant Iowa control with "NO data source identified yet." Chasing that layer (and its provenance in this paper's data-availability statement, retrievable once the PMC embargo lifts 2026-08-09) is a higher-value follow-up than the regionalization claim itself.

SOURCE IDENTIFIED AND NUMBERS VERIFIED EXACT. The DOI resolves to Pandit A., Golden H.E., Christensen J.R., Lane C.R., Husic A. (2025), "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8):e2024WR039207, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207 (US EPA-affiliated authors; PMID 40948694; PMC12425153).

Spatial validation-or prediction in unmonitored basins-yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34)."

So 0.18, 0.34, and "spatial validation / prediction in unmonitored basins" are quoted correctly. The citation is not fabricated and the protocol label is accurate.

WHAT IS REFUTED: the causal mechanism the claim asserts. The claim states the gain came from "restricting the TRAINING POOL" to hydroclimatically similar basins, and concludes this supports "a regionally-specialized model over a continental one." The abstract describes no such experiment. There is ONE model, trained on CONUS-wide sensor data. The 0.18 -> 0.34 difference is an EVALUATION-SUBSET effect: the same continental model's held-out-basin scores are stratified, and the MRB subset of held-out basins scores higher. The paper's own framing is the opposite of the claim's conclusion — spatial validation "guid[ed] the model's targeted application to the MRB," i.e. they retained the CONUS-trained model and applied it to a region where it validated well. No retrained MRB-only model is reported in the abstract, and I could not access the full text to check whether one exists in a supplementary ablation.

CONFOUNDS THE CLAIM IGNORES, even taking 0.18 -> 0.34 at face value: (1) Training-data density, not hydroclimatic similarity, is the more parsimonious explanation — high-frequency nitrate sensors in the US are overwhelmingly concentrated in the Corn Belt/MRB, so MRB held-out basins have far more near-neighbor training basins than, say, arid-West or coastal-Southeast holdouts. That is a coverage effect. (2) KGE is variance- and bias-sensitive; MRB basins have large-amplitude, strongly seasonal nitrate signals, which mechanically inflates KGE relative to low-concentration, low-variance basins elsewhere. Both confounds are consistent with the observed gap without any "regional specialization" mechanism.

n NOT VERIFIABLE. The claim itself concedes n is unknown. The abstract gives no site count, and I could not reach the full text (Wiley 402; PMC embargo lifts 2026-08-09, ~3 weeks from now). - We are ALREADY the restricted case. Their spatial validation is the analogue of our LOFO. Our model is Iowa-only, i.e. we already sit at the maximally regionally-specialized end of the axis the claim recommends moving along. The claim therefore offers no headroom for us; it recommends a move we have already made by construction.
- The paper arguably argues the REVERSE for us. If a CONUS-trained LSTM reaches median spatial KGE 0.34 on MRB ungauged basins, the operative lever is a LARGER training pool of monitored basins spanning the MRB, which is precisely the escape hatch from our n=19-independent-families constraint. Restricting further cannot help; we cannot go below 19.
- Absolute level is weak regardless. Median KGE 0.34 at ungauged basins is modest, and the median hides the lower tail — half of held-out MRB basins did worse. This is consistent with, not a solution to, our between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24).

Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18). Nonetheless, spatial validation was crucial in quantifying the impact of current data gaps and guiding the model's targeted application to the MRB where spatial validation performance was stronger (median KGE = 0.34). ... Interpretable Shapley values identified key spatial drivers influencing mean nitrate concentrations—tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover—and quantitative, non-linear thresholds in their influence, offering management targets."

WHY THE CLAIM IS REFUTED:

1. THE QUOTED SENTENCE IS NOT FROM THIS PAPER. The claim quotes: "developed interpretable random forest models that explain the spatial variation in long-term streamflow, nitrate concentration, and nitrate yield at 95 sites used for model training." The strings "random forest," "streamflow," and "nitrate yield at 95 sites" appear nowhere in the verified abstract. The words "random forest," "XGBoost," and "gradient boosting" do not appear in any accessible metadata for this DOI. I enumerated all 46 OpenAlex-indexed works by Admin Husic and all 15 by Aayush Pandit; none is titled or abstracted as a random-forest paper. Multiple OpenAlex abstract searches for the quoted phrasing ("interpretable random forest models" + nitrate; "nitrate yield" + "random forest"; "nitrate concentration" + "random forest" + "streamflow") returned zero hits. The quote appears to be misattributed to this DOI from some other source, or garbled/fabricated.

2. THE CLAIM'S CORE CHARACTERIZATION IS BACKWARDS. This is not an RF-interpretability paper with no predictive component. It is an LSTM prediction paper. The interpretability layer is SHAPLEY VALUES applied to the deep-learning model, not a random forest.

3. THE CLAIMED SPLIT PROTOCOL ("not-applicable") IS FALSE, AND THIS IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ERROR. The paper's headline structure is precisely a spatial-holdout / prediction-in-ungauged-basins protocol, reported explicitly and quantitatively in the abstract: temporal validation median KGE 0.60 vs SPATIAL validation (unmonitored basins) median KGE 0.18 CONUS-wide and 0.34 restricted to the MRB. The claim asserts the paper contains no spatially-held-out evidence when spatial validation is its central methodological contribution.

4. n = 95 IS UNVERIFIED. The abstract gives no site count. I could not confirm 95 from any accessible source.

WHAT I COULD NOT CHECK (bounds on confidence): full text is inaccessible. Wiley returns HTTP 402/403; the PMC deposit (PMC12425153) is under embargo until 2026-08-09 ("This article will be available in PMC on August 09, 2026"); DOAJ mirror returned 403. So I cannot rule out that the body text contains an RF or XGBoost baseline, a site count of 95, or a head-to-head comparison. The claim's one surviving sliver is that no LSTM-vs-tree head-to-head metric is visible in the abstract or open metadata — that much is true, but it does not rescue a claim whose stated basis describes a paper that does not exist.

TRANSFERABILITY / RELEVANCE TO THE SUSTAG DEPLOYMENT TARGET (the actually useful finding here): this paper is a strong EXTERNAL NEGATIVE RESULT for the ungauged-pin product, and should be cited that way rather than as an LSTM-vs-tree comparison. A well-resourced EPA/academic team with CONUS-wide high-frequency nitrate sensors and a deep sequence model still only reached median KGE 0.18 for daily nitrate concentration at unmonitored basins, improving to 0.34 when the domain was narrowed to the MRB (which contains Iowa). The spatial-vs-temporal gap (0.60 -> 0.18) is the same failure mode this project has already diagnosed: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." That gap appearing independently, in a different modeling family, at continental scale, is evidence the between-site deficit is intrinsic to the ungauged-nitrate problem and not a defect of gradient-boosted trees. Corollary: an LSTM swap is unlikely to close it, and the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint makes a CONUS-trained sequence model doubly implausible here. The paper's Shapley result — that TILE DRAINAGE is a top spatial driver of mean nitrate concentration, with non-linear thresholds — independently corroborates the project's own note that tile drainage density is the dominant missing static control. That is the citable, actionable content of this paper.

DOI 10.1029/2024WR039207 = Pandit A., Golden H.E., Christensen J.R., Lane C.R., Husic A., "Deep Learning Prediction and Interpretation of Riverine Nitrate Export Across the Mississippi River Basin," Water Resources Research 61(8), Aug 2025. PMID 40948694, PMCID PMC12425153. CC-BY-NC gold OA at the publisher, but the Wiley page returns HTTP 402 and the PMC author manuscript is EMBARGOED (efetch shows pmc-status-embargo=yes, pmc-status-live=no; EPA Author Manuscripts collection). Europe PMC has no full-text XML (404). So only the abstract is machine-accessible. Abstract retrieved verbatim and identically from Semantic Scholar Graph API, Europe PMC core record, and NCBI efetch.

THE LOAD-BEARING QUOTATION IS NOT IN THE PAPER'S ACCESSIBLE TEXT. The claim quotes: "developed interpretable random forest models that explain the spatial variation in long-term streamflow, nitrate concentration, and nitrate yield at 95 sites used for model training." Nothing resembling this appears in the abstract. The abstract's interpretability sentence reads: "Interpretable Shapley values identified key spatial drivers influencing mean nitrate concentrations—tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover—and quantitative, non-linear thresholds in their influence, offering management targets." SHAP is model-agnostic; "random forest" is never named. Europe PMC search for "nitrate yield" AND "random forest" AND AUTH:"Pandit" returned hitCount 0; the same query with "95 sites" also returned 0. A scan of all 7 Husic nitrate papers in Europe PMC found no paper matching the quoted description. "Long-term streamflow" as a modeled target does not appear in the abstract at all.

n=95 IS UNSUBSTANTIATED. No site count appears in the abstract. The claim reports "n basins: 95" as if sourced; I could not verify it from any accessible text.

THE STATED SPLIT PROTOCOL IS WRONG, AND THIS IS THE CLAIM'S WORST ERROR. The claim records "split protocol: not-applicable." The paper in fact runs an explicit ungauged-basin (PUB) protocol and reports it in the abstract with hard numbers: temporal validation median KGE = 0.60; "Spatial validation—or prediction in unmonitored basins—yielded lower performance for nitrate concentration (median KGE = 0.18)"; and within the MRB specifically, spatial validation median KGE = 0.34. By declaring the protocol not-applicable, the claim discards the single most decision-relevant fact this paper offers our project.

WHAT SURVIVES. The claim's bottom-line advice — do not cite this paper as evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees for ungauged-basin nitrate — is correct, but for a different reason than the claim gives. It is not that RF was repurposed as an interpretability tool; it is that no RF/XGBoost/gradient-boosting baseline of any kind appears in the accessible text. There is no deep-vs-tree comparison to cite, under any protocol.

TRANSFERABILITY TO OUR SETTING. (a) The KGE = 0.18 CONUS spatial-validation figure is the genuinely citable result here and it independently corroborates our central problem: a well-resourced CONUS-scale LSTM with static attributes transfers poorly to unmonitored basins for nitrate concentration. It is evidence that between-site nitrate transfer is hard in general, not evidence that we should switch architectures. (b) Not comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC / 0.634 PR-AUC: KGE is a continuous hydrograph-similarity metric on daily concentration, wrong for our binary daily-exceedance target, and it is computed per-site then medianed. Do not place KGE 0.18 next to our between_r2 0.21 as if they measure the same thing. (c) Data overlap, not independent replication: their training data are high-frequency nitrate sensors across the CONUS, which necessarily include the USGS and Iowa (IWQIS) sensors our 85 sites are drawn from. This is largely the same signal, so it cannot serve as external validation of our numbers. (d) n=19 constraint: their spatial-validation site pool is of the same order of magnitude as ours (tens of sensor sites, not CAMELS-scale 531-671 basins), so this paper does NOT demonstrate a method that needs hundreds of catchments — but it also does not demonstrate one that works at small n, since its ungauged-basin performance was weak. (e) Genuinely actionable side-finding: SHAP identified TILE DRAINAGE as a top spatial driver of mean nitrate concentration, with non-linear thresholds. That is exactly the dominant control our feature set is missing, and it implies Pandit et al. sourced a CONUS or MRB-wide tile-drainage layer. Chasing that layer (likely via the paper's data-availability statement once the embargo lifts 2026-04-16, or by emailing husic@vt.edu) is a higher-value follow-up than anything about LSTM-vs-trees.

tier3_unverified.claim: THE HEADLINE RESULT IS NOT AN UNGAUGED-BASIN RESULT. In Figs. 3 and 6, LSTMs trained regionally are always TESTED ON THE SAME BASINS THEY WERE TRAINED ON, during a different time period. Verbatim from Sect. 4: 'This was done using k-fold cross-validation so that all models were tested on the same basin(s) where they were trained (during different time periods)'; Fig. 6 caption repeats 'All models were tested on the same basins where they were trained (during different time periods).' The paper's conclusion — train on hundreds of basins — is thus established under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one, and its effect sizes are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — protocol claim

tier3_unverified.claim: The 'how many basins are necessary' ablation (Fig. 6, blue line) partitions the 531 CAMELS basins into random disjoint groups of ~6 sizes (roughly 50, 20, 10, 5, 3, 2 groups, i.e. group sizes from single basins up to 531), trains a 10-member LSTM ensemble per group on 1999-2008 and tests on 1989-1999. Median NSE over 531 basins rises MONOTONICALLY with training-set size all the way to 531 basins, with no plateau: 'even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow.' CRITICAL for us: the paper reports these medians ONLY as a figure curve — no numeric median NSE values are given in the text, tables, or appendices, so the effect size cannot be quoted, and no minimum-viable basin count is ever stated.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: monotonic increase in median NSE with number of training basins; exact values not reported numerically anywhere in the paper (figure-only)

In Fig. 3a, conceptual (mHM) and process-based (VIC) models calibrated PER BASIN outperform the same models calibrated regionally across 489 CAMELS basins; in Fig. 3b, LSTMs trained on all 531 basins outperform 531 separately-trained single-basin LSTMs. The paper asserts the per-basin-beats-regional result for conceptual models is 'a consistent finding across hydrological-modeling studies (e.g., Beck et al., 2016; Mizukami et al., 2017).' This implies the large-n benefit is specific to high-capacity sequence models that must learn shared representation, and does not automatically transfer to a per-site-tuned or low-capacity model class such as a boosted tree.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: CDF crossover shown in Fig. 3a vs 3b; no numeric medians reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (LSTM), 489 (mHM/VIC)

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON HYDROLOGICALLY-INFORMED SUBSETTING, directly relevant to our n=19 families. Training on hydrologically coherent subsets of CAMELS — 18 USGS HUC regions (2 to 79 basins each) or 6 k-means clusters of 25 static catchment attributes (59 to 195 basins each) — produced models that were BETTER than random basin groups of the same size but STILL WORSE ON AVERAGE than the single model trained on all 531 basins: 'models trained on any subset of the 531 CAMELS basins performed worse, on average, than models trained on all 531 CAMELS basins.' Fig. 7 (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank over 10 repetitions, alpha=0.05): 'All models perform worse than the full regional model in more basins than they perform better in.' The paper also explicitly disclaims relevance to PUB: 'this analysis does not account for the value of hydrologic diversity for prediction in ungauged basins.'
tier3_unverified.effectSize: every subset-trained model statistically worse in more basins than better (Wilcoxon, alpha=0.05, 10 reps); numeric NSE deltas not reported

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON PREDICTING WHICH MODEL WINS WHERE, and on hybrid/physics-informed models. The authors state they 'tried extensively to construct a separate predictor model that uses catchment attributes and/or hydrological signatures to predict whether one model will perform better or worse than other models in specific basins. We have not been able to construct a model that performs well at this task,' and that training-period or validation-period metrics cannot reliably select the best model for the test period. Separately, on hybrid differentiable models: 'so far, to our knowledge, all attempts to add physics to (properly trained) streamflow LSTM models in hydrology have produced lower-performing models.' Both are unquantified assertions in an opinion paper with no supporting experiment reported, and the physics claim carries the escape hatch 'properly trained'.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: none reported — qualitative assertions, no supporting numbers or ablation in the paper

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019, WRR 10.1029/2019WR026065) trained LSTMs on 531 CAMELS basins with k=12-fold basin holdout so predictions were made in basins supplying no training data. The out-of-sample 'PUB LSTM' 10-member ensemble achieved median NSE 0.69 (mean 0.54, min -13.02, max 0.90) versus 0.64 median for per-basin-calibrated SAC-SMA (mean 0.51) and 0.58 for the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis (mean 0.31). PUB LSTM beat SAC-SMA in 307/531 (58%) catchments and the NWM in 347/531 (66%). CRITICAL LIMITATION for our use: the target is DAILY STREAMFLOW, not any water-quality or nutrient concentration variable, and NO machine-learning baseline was tested — both benchmarks are process-based hydrologic models. The paper therefore provides ZERO evidence that LSTM beats gradient-boosted trees at anything.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median NSE: PUB LSTM 0.69 vs SAC-SMA 0.64 vs NWM 0.58; win rate 58% and 66% of 531 basins

tier3_unverified.claim: The spatial holdout in Kratzert et al. (2019) is a RANDOM k=12-fold split of the 531 CAMELS basins, not a leave-one-region-out or leave-one-basin-family-out split. Exact text: 'Out-of-sample testing was done by k-fold validation, which splits the 531 basins randomly into k = 12 groups of approximately equal size.' With ~44 held-out basins per fold drawn randomly from across CONUS, every held-out basin retains many hydro-climatically and geographically similar donor basins in the ~487-basin training set. This is a WEAKER transfer test than our LOFO protocol, which groups nested/temporally-overlapping basins into 19 families. The reported 0.69 NSE therefore does NOT establish that LSTM PUB gains persist under leave-one-REGION-out, and the paper reports no region-level or spatially-blocked variant.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — protocol characterization
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 basins split into 12 random folds (~44 held out per fold)

tier3_unverified.claim: In Kratzert et al. (2019), essentially all between-site skill came from STATIC catchment attributes, not from temporal dynamics. The Global LSTM trained on all basins WITHOUT static attributes reached median NSE 0.63 (mean 0.45); adding the CAMELS static attributes (soils, climate, vegetation, topography, geology) raised it to median NSE 0.74 (mean 0.68) — a gain of +0.11 median NSE, statistically significant at p < 0.05 (Wilcoxon). Separately, the cost of going ungauged was small: gauged Global LSTM with statics 0.74 vs ungauged PUB LSTM 0.69, only -0.05 median NSE. This independently corroborates the sustag finding that the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE STATIC information, and implies that on this project static-attribute enrichment (tile drainage, soils, geology) is the higher-value lever than any sequence architecture.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: +0.11 median NSE from static catchment attributes (0.63 -> 0.74); only -0.05 median NSE penalty for ungauged vs gauged (0.74 -> 0.69)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout for the 0.69 PUB number; the 0.63 and 0.74 Global LSTM numbers are temporal-holdout on all 531 in-sample basins (train 1981-1995, test 1996-2010) and are NOT spatially held out

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019) contains NO ablation of performance versus the NUMBER OF TRAINING BASINS. Every LSTM configuration is trained on ~487 basins (11 of 12 folds) or all 531; there is no experiment at reduced basin counts and no statement of a minimum viable basin count. The paper's own causal claim is that success depends on training over 'large, diverse data sets' — its conclusion 3 reads that there is 'sufficient information contained in catchment attribute data to distinguish between different rainfall-runoff relationships in at least most of the US catchments that we tested.' At n=19 independent basin families, the sustag project sits roughly 25x below this paper's basin count, and this paper offers no evidence that the reported PUB advantage survives that reduction.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: absence of evidence — no basin-count ablation exists in this paper

Modelling & Software, S136481522030983X), same 531 CAMELS basins. Median NSE by (training years, basins): at 3yr/13 basins XGBoost 0.41 vs EA-LSTM 0.43; 3yr/53 0.48 vs 0.56; 3yr/531 0.57 vs 0.68; 9yr/13 0.54 vs 0.63; 9yr/53 0.61 vs 0.68; 9yr/531 0.66 vs 0.74. The authors state that at the small configurations 'three to six years and 13 basins, XGBoost and EA-LSTM result in NSE distributions that do not differ significantly (large p-values)', and that 'the effect size d grows with the number of basins, but has no clear relationship to the number of training years.' The deep model's advantage is therefore driven by BASIN COUNT, not record length — the exact axis on which sustag is starved (19 families) and rich (18 years, 160k site-days).

tier3_unverified.claim: Two further cautions against a deep-model pivot at small n. (1) Gauch et al. (arXiv:1911.07249) report that a prior study by the same group, Gauch et al. (2019a), 'found the GBRT-framework XGBoost to provide more accurate predictions than LSTMs' — a published negative result for LSTM in a rainfall-runoff setting. (2) Kratzert et al. (2019) document severe seed-level instability in ungauged LSTM prediction: across the 531 basins, 103 basins had at least one of the 10 PUB LSTM ensemble members score NSE < 0; only 9 of those 103 had all 10 members below zero, and 55 of the 103 had at least one member above NSE 0.5. One basin (USGS 01142500) had 9 of 10 members at NSE < 0 and one member above 0.7. The authors conclude 'a substantial portion of the uncertainty in these LSTM models is due to randomness, rather than to systematic model structural error', which is why they ensemble N=10. Any LSTM attempt on sustag must budget for multi-seed ensembling, and with only 19 held-out families the per-fold seed variance would likely swamp the effect being measured.

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019, WRR, doi:10.1029/2019WR026065), the anchor PUB result cited by the Willard et al. survey, trained an entity-aware LSTM on 531 CAMELS catchments (4-2,000 km2, ~30 yr daily data) under k-fold SPATIAL cross-validation so that every prediction basin supplied zero training data. Ungauged-basin median NSE = 0.69, which EXCEEDED the calibrated SAC-SMA (0.64) and the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis (0.58) evaluated in GAUGED mode over a 15-year period. FALSIFIABLE/RELEVANCE CAVEATS: (a) the target is daily STREAMFLOW, not a water-quality concentration; (b) the evidence base is n=531 independent catchments, ~28x our 19 independent basin families, so this result provides no support for a deep-model advantage at n=19; (c) no gradient-boosted-tree baseline was run — the comparison is LSTM vs process-based models, not LSTM vs XGBoost. Predicts nothing about whether an LSTM would beat our booster.

tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (CAMELS)

FALSIFIABLE: no metric, split protocol, or site count is attached to this XGBoost comparison in the survey. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION for this project: pretraining a deep model on a large external basin corpus (e.g. CAMELS, CAMELS-Chem) and fine-tuning to Iowa is NOT reliably better than a model fit directly on the local data — the one large-scale transfer experiment the survey cites found the opposite direction. This weakens the main proposed route by which the n=531-basin deep-learning literature could be imported to an n=19 problem.

tier3_unverified.claim: GRAPH NEURAL NETWORKS ARE NOT A SAFE BET AND MOST VARIANTS CANNOT SERVE THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: the survey reports that for river-network modeling 'ChebNet-LSTM and GCN-LSTM performed worse ... than the standard LSTM and GraphWaveNet was the only one that performed better,' i.e. 2 of 3 GNN architectures LOST to a plain LSTM. Critically, the survey distinguishes TRANSDUCTIVE GNNs (require the test node to be present in the graph at training time) from INDUCTIVE GNNs, which 'are built using only training entities and allow for new entity nodes to be integrated during testing.' FALSIFIABLE DEPLOYMENT CONSTRAINT: an arbitrary Iowa map pin is a node that did not exist at training time, so ONLY inductive architectures (GraphWaveNet-class, or an encoder over static attributes) are admissible; any transductive GCN/ChebNet result in the literature is inapplicable to this product regardless of its reported accuracy. The survey's recommended cheap middle ground is entity-aware modeling — either direct concatenation of static site characteristics to dynamic inputs (which 'does not require novel ML architecture and is therefore very accessible', and is what our booster already does) or a learned ENCODING of static characteristics via a separate network, which the survey reports gave only a 'slight improvement over the static and dynamic concatenation approach' (Tayal et al., lake temperature). Predicted effect of adding a site-embedding/encoder layer on top of our existing static features: SMALL, and the survey provides no numeric gain for it.

tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — river-network reach count not stated in the survey text retrieved; lake-temperature meta-learning study used 305 target lakes treated as unmonitored in the Upper Midwestern US

tier3_unverified.claim: Xiong et al. (2022) trained their LSTM on a SINGLE watershed — the North River Watershed (NRW), a subbasin of the Jiulong River, Fujian Province, China — not on a multi-basin corpus. Inputs were hydrometeorological data plus anthropogenic nitrogen sources (fertilizer application and livestock breeding). This means the paper is NOT evidence that LSTMs learn cross-site absolute level from many basins; it is a single-basin model tested for transfer. Falsifiable: if the full text shows the LSTM was trained on multiple gauged watersheds simultaneously, this claim is wrong.
