tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 training watershed (North River Watershed, Jiulong River, China); 7 additional watersheds used only as transfer targets

tier3_unverified.claim: The transfer experiment in Xiong et al. (2022) was conducted on the FLUX model, not the concentration model: 'The flux model ensemble, without retraining, performed well (mean NSE = 0.32–0.84) in seven distinct watersheds in Asia, Europe, and North America.' The abstract and both institutional press releases describe only flux transfer; no published number exists for transferred CONCENTRATION performance. Since daily flux = concentration x discharge, and the paper attributes interbasin consistency to 'similarities in rainfall-runoff relationships', the transferable skill is plausibly hydrologic (discharge dynamics) rather than concentration-level skill. Falsifiable: if the SI reports transferred concentration NSE, this claim is wrong.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: mean NSE 0.32–0.84 across 7 watersheds for FLUX; no reported transferred concentration NSE
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (no target-basin training data), but transfer of a single-basin model
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 7 transfer-target watersheds

tier3_unverified.claim: Xiong et al. (2022) reports NO head-to-head comparison against gradient-boosted trees, random forests, or any other machine-learning baseline. The only comparison stated is rhetorical and against process-based models: the LSTM performance is 'a performance unlikely to be achieved by generic process-based models with comparable data quality.' The HKUST press release confirms 'no specific baseline model comparison results.' Therefore this paper CANNOT be cited as evidence that LSTM beats XGBoost for ungauged-basin water-quality prediction. Falsifiable: if the full text contains an RF/XGBoost benchmark table, this claim is wrong.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no ML baseline reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: n/a

tier3_unverified.claim: Zero-shot spatial transfer of the Xiong LSTM failed badly in the one North American, human-dominated target: the Newport Bay Watershed (USA) scored NSE = 0.32 while the other six watersheds scored mean NSE 0.55–0.84. Retraining WITH multi-watershed data raised that lowest NSE from 0.32 to 0.68. This is a negative result for pure transfer and a positive result for pooled multi-basin training — but the fix required adding target-region data, which for an arbitrary Iowa map pin is exactly what is unavailable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: NSE 0.32 -> 0.68 after retraining with multi-watershed data (flux)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout for the NSE=0.32 zero-shot number; the 0.68 figure is NOT spatially held out (target-region data included in retraining)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 7 transfer targets; worst case n=1 (Newport Bay, USA)

tier3_unverified.claim: Xiong et al. (2022) predicts DIN concentration and flux at a river outlet as a continuous daily time series, not exceedance of a regulatory threshold, and the headline NSE values are computed against a discharge-weighted flux target. NSE on flux is inflated relative to concentration skill because flux is dominated by discharge variance; the same model scored NSE 0.92 on flux but only 0.67 on concentration in the SAME basin under the SAME split. Any citation of the '0.92' figure as evidence of nitrogen-chemistry skill is a protocol/target mismatch with a concentration or violation-classification target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: NSE 0.92 (flux) vs 0.67 (concentration), same basin, same split — a 0.25 NSE gap purely from target definition
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 (home basin)

tier3_unverified.claim: FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, DIFFERENT SOURCE (Pandit et al. 2025, Water Resources Research, doi:10.1029/2024WR039207): an LSTM trained on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across the CONUS (n=95 sites; n=50 within the Mississippi River Basin) achieved median KGE 0.60 under TEMPORAL validation but median KGE only 0.18 under SPATIAL cross-validation (whole watersheds withheld = prediction in ungauged basins), improving to median KGE 0.34 when restricted to Mississippi River Basin sites. This is the closest available analogue to the Iowa deployment target and shows an LSTM at n=95 sites collapsing under spatial holdout for nitrate CONCENTRATION — direct evidence AGAINST expecting an LSTM to solve the between-site problem at n=19 families. Metrics taken from the article landing page/abstract, not the full text; verify against the paper before citing.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 temporal vs 0.18 spatial for daily nitrate concentration — a 0.42 KGE drop from changing only the split protocol
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: both reported separately: temporal-holdout (median KGE 0.60) and spatial-holdout / leave-watershed-out PUB (median KGE 0.18 CONUS, 0.34 MRB)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 95 CONUS sensor sites; 50 in the Mississippi River Basin

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) contains NO spatial-holdout / ungauged-basin experiment. The companion USGS data release's FGDC data dictionary defines the split variable verbatim as: 'Train/Val/Test — A label indicating if the observation/prediction falls into the training validation or prediction TIME PERIOD as defined by the run config file.' All 46 sites appear in training in every one of the four modeling schemes (single-site, cluster, hydro-terrane, global); held-out data are later years at sites the model has already seen. Consequently none of this paper's KGE values are comparable to a leave-one-basin-out number, and the paper provides zero evidence about LSTM performance at an unmonitored map pin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — protocol finding, not a performance number

tier3_unverified.claim: Pooling sites into a single global LSTM DEGRADED accuracy relative to per-site models for stream nitrate. Across 46 sites: 46 single-site models achieved median KGE = 0.66 (median RMSE = 1.06 mg/L; 32 of 46 sites, 70%, had KGE > 0.5); 5 cluster models (sites grouped by basin attributes) achieved median KGE = 0.66; the single global model trained on all 46 sites achieved median KGE = 0.63. The abstract states 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model.' This is a direct negative result for the assumption that more pooled basins buys transfer skill for nutrient concentration.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: global median KGE 0.63 vs single-site 0.66 vs cluster 0.66 — pooling cost ~0.03 KGE and hurt distinctive sites specifically
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 46 (46 single-site models; 5 clusters; 8 hydro terranes; 1 global)

tier3_unverified.claim: The authors explicitly deny that the streamflow-domain 'global model beats local model' finding (Kratzert-style) transfers to water quality: 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' Elsewhere they note that in contrast to discharge modeling, where larger multi-catchment datasets improved deep learning performance, for water quality 'smaller groups of catchments or even single-catchment models [are] currently being equally effective for capturing nutrient dynamics.' This is a peer-reviewed statement that the CAMELS-scale (531-671 basin) deep-learning evidence base should NOT be assumed to carry over to nitrate.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative claim by authors, supported by their 0.63 global vs 0.66 local result

tier3_unverified.claim: Every one of the 46 sites is a USGS NWIS station with a CO-LOCATED DISCHARGE GAUGE, and daily discharge (NWIS parameter code 00060) is a required model input alongside nitrate (code 99133); the FGDC attribute table lists discharge ranging 0–192,000 cfs. The paper's headline conclusion is that 'discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes show a particularly strong influence on model performance' — i.e. the strongest single driver of the model is an input that is unavailable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin. The reported KGE 0.63–0.66 numbers therefore cannot be reproduced by any weather-and-land-use-only model, and this paper offers no discharge-free ablation to bound how much skill would be lost.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: discharge is the top-ranked driver; no discharge-free variant reported

tier3_unverified.claim: The study compares only LSTM variants against each other (single-site vs 5-cluster vs 8-hydro-terrane vs global). It reports NO random forest, XGBoost, gradient-boosted-tree, or linear regression baseline anywhere in the paper or in the released code archive (whose 02_run_model directory contains only PyTorch model_weights.pt outputs and LSTM run/model config YAMLs). Therefore this paper provides no evidence that LSTMs beat gradient-boosted trees for nitrate, under any split protocol.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: zero GBDT/RF baselines present

tier3_unverified.claim: Design details usable as a template: 46 predominantly agricultural sites across the midwestern and eastern US (bounding box -96.75 to -74.22 lon, 38.32 to 44.53 lat), data period 2010-01-01 to 2021-12-31, target = 7-day backward-looking average nitrate (NO3-N + NO2-N, observed range -0.1 to 30.9 mg/L). Static attributes span anthropogenic hydrologic modification, nitrogen application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, watershed physical attributes, and soils. Feature importance was computed as permuted-RMSE / baseline-RMSE averaged over 10 replicates (reported range -0.09 to 9.82). Sites were grouped two ways for pooling: 5 attribute-based clusters and 8 glacial hydrogeologic 'hydro terranes' — a grouping strategy directly analogous to, and validating, the basin-family grouping approach, at a scale (46 sites → 5 or 8 groups) comparable to the 85 sites → 19 families constraint.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: grouping by similarity raised accuracy at poorly-performing sites while full pooling lowered it
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 46 sites, grouped into 5 clusters or 8 hydro terranes

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019, 10.1029/2019WR026065) report that an LSTM predicting in basins that supplied ZERO training data ('PUB LSTM', 10-member ensemble, inputs = 5 NLDAS daily meteorological forcings + 27 static CAMELS catchment attributes, 256 cell states, dropout 0.4) achieved median NSE 0.69 over 531 CAMELS catchments in water years 1996-2010, versus 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated SEPARATELY IN EACH BASIN on 15 years of that basin's own data and 0.58 for the NOAA National Water Model reanalysis. The PUB LSTM beat SAC-SMA in 307 of 531 catchments (58%) and the NWM in 347 of 531 (66%). This is the headline evidence that a spatially-transferred deep model can beat locally-calibrated process models — but note the target is STREAMFLOW, not any water-quality or concentration variable, and no gradient-boosted-tree, random-forest, or any other ML baseline appears anywhere in the paper.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: PUB LSTM median NSE 0.69 vs calibrated SAC-SMA 0.64 (+0.05) vs NWM 0.58 (+0.11); win rate 307/531 and 347/531
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 CAMELS catchments (subset of 671; 4-2000 km2), ~30 years daily data each; train 1981-1995, test 1996-2010

tier3_unverified.claim: The spatial holdout in Kratzert et al. (2019) is k-fold with k=12 where the 531 basins were split RANDOMLY into 12 groups of approximately equal size (~44 held out, ~487 used for training each fold) — the paper states this explicitly ('splits the 531 basins randomly into k = 12 groups'). Groups were NOT formed by region, watershed nesting, hydrologic unit, or any spatial-blocking rule, so every held-out basin almost certainly had geographically and climatically adjacent basins in its own training set. The paper contains NO leave-one-region-out experiment and no analysis of whether the 0.69 median NSE degrades as the held-out basin's distance or dissimilarity from the nearest training basin increases. Therefore this number is NOT directly comparable to a leave-one-basin-FAMILY-out protocol that removes nested/overlapping neighbors, and it should be treated as an upper bound on what random-basin-holdout can show about true regional transfer.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — protocol characterization; no region-blocked variant reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 total; k=12 random folds, ~44 test / ~487 train per fold

tier3_unverified.claim: In Kratzert et al. (2019), STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES — not temporal dynamics — are what makes cross-basin transfer work. Two LSTMs trained on all 531 basins with identical meteorological forcings differ only in whether the 27 static attributes are appended at each timestep: median NSE 0.74 WITH statics vs 0.63 WITHOUT (+0.11 NSE; the authors state the NSE difference was statistically significant at p < 1e-9). Correspondingly, the fully out-of-sample PUB LSTM (0.69) gave up only 0.05 median NSE relative to the in-sample Global LSTM with statics (0.74), i.e. most of the achievable skill survives never having seen the basin — the transferable information lives in the static descriptors. The 27 attributes span climate indices (aridity, precip seasonality, snow fraction, high/low precip frequency and duration), topography (elevation, slope, area), vegetation (forest fraction, LAI max, LAI difference, GVF max/difference), SOIL (depth to bedrock, soil depth, porosity, saturated hydraulic conductivity, max water content, sand/silt/clay fractions) and GEOLOGY (carbonate rock fraction, log10 surface permeability).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: statics vs no-statics: median NSE 0.74 vs 0.63 (+0.11), p<1e-9; in-sample-to-PUB penalty only 0.74->0.69 (-0.05)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (both global LSTM variants trained on all basins, in-sample); PUB LSTM 531 under k=12 holdout

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019) report a heavy left tail for the ungauged LSTM that the median conceals: PUB LSTM mean NSE 0.54 versus median 0.69, with minimum NSE -13.02 (Table 2, 531 catchments). The authors state 'SAC-SMA tended to out-perform the PUB LSTM in catchments with low NSE values' — i.e. the locally-calibrated conceptual model was MORE robust exactly where the transferred deep model failed. They also report a negative result on static attributes: adding catchment attributes HURT the model in some catchments, and 'there is generally no correlation between the values of individual catchment attributes and whether the Global LSTM with vs. without statics performs better' (their Figure 5), so they could not diagnose which attribute or which catchment type causes the degradation; their tentative explanation is error/uncertainty in the attribute data itself. Comparable spread for other models: SAC-SMA median 0.64 / mean 0.51 / min -12.28; Global LSTM without statics median 0.63 / mean 0.45 / min -31.72; NWM median 0.58 / mean 0.31 / min -20.28.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: PUB LSTM mean 0.54 vs median 0.69, min -13.02; SAC-SMA wins in the low-NSE tail (SAC-SMA better in 224/531 = 42% of catchments)

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019) found that a large fraction of ungauged-LSTM failure is RANDOM SEED, not model structure, and that single-model results are therefore untrustworthy: across the 10-member PUB LSTM ensemble, 103 of 531 basins had at least one ensemble member with NSE below zero, yet only 9 of those 103 had all 10 members below zero, and 55 of the 103 had at least one member with NSE > 0.5. In one named basin (USGS 01142500), 9 of 10 members scored NSE < 0 while one member scored NSE > 0.7. All reported LSTM metrics are computed from the mean of the 10-member ensemble (chosen to match the 10 SCE random restarts used to calibrate SAC-SMA). Practical implication for any small-n deep-learning attempt: a single training run's held-out score can be off by more than the entire claimed advantage over the benchmark, so seed-ensembling is mandatory and a one-seed LSTM-vs-XGBoost comparison would be uninterpretable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 103/531 basins have >=1 of 10 seeds with NSE<0; only 9/531 have all 10 seeds NSE<0; 55/103 have >=1 seed NSE>0.5
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531; ensemble N=10

tier3_unverified.claim: The Kratzert 2019 PUB result rests on a training set roughly four orders of magnitude larger in INDEPENDENT SPATIAL UNITS than a 19-basin-family problem: ~487 training basins per fold x ~15 years of daily data (approximately 2.7 million basin-days per fold, ~5.8 million basin-days across the full 30-year record). The paper offers no experiment at reduced basin count. The follow-up literature that does test this reports the scaling is still climbing at CAMELS scale: Gauch, Klotz, Nearing, Kratzert et al., 'HESS Opinions: Never train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network on a single basin' (HESS 28:4187, 2024, doi 10.5194/hess-28-4187-2024) trains LSTMs on random groups of approximately 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50 basins plus the full 531 and reports median NSE rising monotonically with training-set size, 'continuing up to the maximum size of the CAMELS data set (531 basins)' with no plateau — exact per-group NSE values are shown only in their Figure 6, not tabulated in text. Their companion conclusion is that for LSTMs, regional models beat single-basin models while for conceptual/process models the reverse holds. At 19 independent basin families this places any LSTM/EA-LSTM proposal at the extreme low end of a curve that had not yet flattened at 531 basins; neither paper compares LSTM against XGBoost, random forest, or any gradient-boosted baseline at ANY basin count, so there is no published evidence in this line of work that a deep sequence model beats a booster in the small-n regime.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median NSE increases monotonically with training basin count through 531 with no observed plateau; exact values figure-only
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Kratzert 2019: ~487 train / ~44 test per fold of 531. Gauch et al. 2024 ablation: ~2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 531 basins

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089) did NOT perform any ungauged-basin / spatially held-out experiment. Training and evaluation used the SAME 531 CAMELS basins, separated only in time (calibration/training 1 Oct 1999 - 30 Sep 2008; evaluation 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999). The paper explicitly states 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data.' Therefore NONE of this paper's headline NSE numbers are comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC, and this paper is NOT evidence that EA-LSTM transfers to an unseen basin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not applicable - protocol claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 basins trained; 447 basins used for the benchmark comparison (CAMELS, CONUS)

tier3_unverified.claim: Under that temporal-holdout protocol, an 8-member EA-LSTM ensemble reached median NSE ~0.74 (single EA-LSTM models: mean NSE 0.67 +/- 0.006, median ~0.71), exceeding process-based models calibrated INDIVIDUALLY per basin (mHM basin-calibrated median NSE ~0.68; HBV upper-bound, 100 calibration trials, median ~0.68). Caveat: exact Table 3 figures were extracted via an HTML render, not the PDF (PDF fetch returned unparseable binary), so individual model rows should be verified against the published Table 3 before citation.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: EA-LSTM ensemble median NSE ~0.74 vs ~0.68 for the best basin-calibrated conceptual models (delta ~ +0.06 NSE)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 447 benchmark basins (of 531 trained)

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper contains NO comparison to random forests, gradient-boosted trees, or any tree ensemble. Every baseline is either a process-based hydrologic model (SAC-SMA+Snow-17, VIC, mHM, HBV, FUSE) or another LSTM variant. This paper therefore provides ZERO evidence that LSTM/EA-LSTM outperforms XGBoost, and it cannot be cited to justify replacing a gradient-boosted model.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: zero tree-ensemble baselines present

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper contains NO ablation on the number of training basins. Performance is reported only for the single configuration trained on all 531 basins simultaneously; there is no curve or table of accuracy versus training-basin count. Consequently this paper gives NO evidence that EA-LSTM's regional-embedding advantage survives at n=19 independent basin families, and its entire evidence base is 28x larger than our effective sample.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no scaling analysis exists
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (single configuration only; not varied)

tier3_unverified.claim: Process-based models calibrated REGIONALLY (i.e. one parameter set transferred across basins, the closest analogue to our between-site problem) collapse relative to per-basin calibration: VIC regional mean NSE 0.17 / median 0.31 versus basin-calibrated performance in the ~0.6-0.68 range; mHM regional mean 0.44 / median 0.53. This independently corroborates that the between-site / absolute-level term is the hard part of the problem, and that it is hard for physically-based models too, not just for our booster.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: VIC median NSE 0.31 (regional) vs ~0.68 (basin-calibrated): loss of ~0.37 NSE. mHM 0.53 vs ~0.68.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (regional vs basin-specific calibration, all basins seen in training)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 447 benchmark basins

tier3_unverified.claim: The EA-LSTM's mechanism is a static-attribute embedding: 27 CAMELS catchment attributes (climate indices, vegetation indices, soil and topographic properties, chosen as the subset derivable from remote sensing or CONUS-wide products) are mapped through a learned input gate into an R^256 embedding, and k-means clustering of that embedding reproduces hydrologically coherent basin groups. The highest-ranked attributes were mean elevation, catchment area, mean precipitation, aridity (PET/P), duration of high-precipitation events, fraction of precipitation as snow, and forest fraction; soil properties ranked lower. This is a direct argument that BETWEEN-SITE static geography carries the transferable signal - consistent with our own finding that only geometry/static-geography features have produced wins - but it is a learned 256-d embedding fit on 531 basins and is very unlikely to be identifiable from 19 families.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 27 static attributes -> R^256 embedding

tier3_unverified.claim: The ACTUAL spatially-held-out evidence is in the companion paper, Kratzert, Klotz, Herrnegger, Sampson, Hochreiter & Nearing (2019), 'Toward Improved Predictions in Ungauged Basins: Exploiting the Power of Machine Learning', Water Resources Research 55(12):11344-11354, DOI 10.1029/2019WR026065. Using k-fold (k=12) SPATIAL cross-validation over 531 CAMELS basins so that predictions are made in basins supplying no training data, the out-of-sample LSTM achieved median NSE 0.69, versus 0.64 for SAC-SMA calibrated AT the target gauge and 0.58 for the National Water Model. Note the training set per fold is still ~487 basins; the folds are random basin splits, NOT leave-one-region-out, so spatial-proximity leakage across folds is not excluded. This paper (not the HESS one) is the correct citation for PUB claims, and it also contains no tree-ensemble baseline and no training-basin-count ablation.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: out-of-sample LSTM median NSE 0.69 vs locally-calibrated SAC-SMA 0.64 vs National Water Model 0.58
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (k=12-fold basin-wise cross-validation; random basin folds, not region-wise)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 CAMELS basins; ~487 training basins per fold

tier3_unverified.claim: LSTM streamflow skill increases MONOTONICALLY with the number of training basins across groupings of [2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, ..., 531] basins, with NO observed plateau: 'The blue line in Fig. 6 shows performance (median NSE) increasing as the size of the training data set increases. This effect continues up to the maximum size of the CAMELS data set (531 basins). In other words, it is better to have more basins in the training set, and even these 531 basins are most likely not to be enough to train optimal LSTM models for streamflow.' FALSIFIABLE AND DIRECTLY ADVERSE TO OUR PROJECT: our 19 independent basin families sit at the far-left, worst-performing end of this curve. The paper identifies no minimum viable n but explicitly demands 'at least hundreds of basins.' If the curve has not asymptoted by 531, an LSTM trained on 19 families is deep in the regime the authors characterize as an 'improperly trained model.' NOTE: this is a STREAMFLOW result, not water quality, and the curve is measured under temporal holdout, not spatial holdout.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Direction and monotonicity stated in text and shown in Fig. 6; the paper reports NO numeric median NSE values anywhere in text or captions - only CDF/curve graphics. Effect magnitude is therefore NOT extractable from the HTML.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (train 1999-2008; test 1989-1999; 'All models were tested on the same basins where they were trained (during different time periods)') - explicitly NOT spatial holdout
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (CAMELS-US), partitioned into k-fold groups of size ~2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 107, ..., up to 531; 10-member ensemble at each grouping size

tier3_unverified.claim: THIS PAPER CONTAINS NO UNGAUGED-BASIN / PUB / SPATIAL-HOLDOUT EXPERIMENT. Every reported result trains and tests on the same basins in different time windows. The paper cites Kratzert et al. (2019) ungauged-basin work but quotes NO numbers from it (no LSTM-vs-calibrated-SAC-SMA NSE comparison is reproduced). Consequently, this source provides ZERO evidence bearing on our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin) and none of its numbers may be compared to our LOFO AUC 0.820. Anyone citing this paper as evidence that LSTMs transfer to unseen basins is misreading it.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not-applicable
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout throughout; no spatial holdout exists in the paper
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (all in-sample)

tier3_unverified.claim: Training on a HYDROLOGICALLY HOMOGENEOUS subset is worse than training on a heterogeneous full sample: 'models trained on any subset of the 531 CAMELS basins performed worse, on average, than models trained on all 531 CAMELS basins.' This was tested two ways - (a) grouping by USGS Hydrologic Unit Code, 18 HUCs with 2-79 basins each, and (b) k-means clustering on 25 basin attributes, 6 clusters with 59-195 basins each. Both underperformed the all-531 model. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR US: restricting a model to Iowa-like basins, or clustering our 19 families into hydrologic sub-groups before fitting, is predicted to HURT, not help. It also implies the fix for our between-site deficit is to ENLARGE the basin sample (e.g. by pulling in out-of-state nitrate monitoring sites), not to specialize the model to Iowa.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Direction stated ('performed worse, on average'); no numeric median NSE deltas given in text or Fig. 6 caption
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (tested on same basins as trained, different period)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 total; HUC groups 2-79 basins; attribute clusters 59-195 basins

tier3_unverified.claim: Regional (multi-basin) training reverses the sign of the single-basin-vs-regional comparison relative to process-based models. For conceptual/process models (VIC and mHM, 489 CAMELS basins), single-basin calibration BEATS regional calibration; for LSTMs (531 basins) the opposite holds - 'In Fig. 3a, single-basin models perform better than regional models, and in Fig. 3b, this is reversed.' The paper states that process models performing worse under regional calibration 'is, to our knowledge, a consistent finding.' FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: the 'pool all sites into one model' strategy we already use is the correct one for a learned model, and per-site models are the wrong direction - but this says nothing about whether a per-site EMBEDDING or random effect helps, which the paper does not test.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Sign reversal reported via cumulative density functions (Fig. 3a vs 3b); no numeric NSE values stated
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (LSTM); 489 (VIC and mHM benchmark runs)

tier3_unverified.claim: Single-basin-trained LSTMs catastrophically fail at extrapolating beyond the range seen in their own training record: across 531 single-basin models, 'there are more than 6346 flow values above the theoretical maximums of their respective single-basin models,' versus only 10 such values for the single regional model trained on all 531 basins. This is a ~635x reduction in out-of-range failures from pooling. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR OUR CLASSIFIER: a model with few effective training units cannot predict magnitudes it has never observed - which is precisely our between-site failure mode (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21). It supports the diagnosis that our absolute-level deficit is a SAMPLE-COVERAGE problem (19 families spanning too narrow a range of basin types), not an architecture problem.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: >6346 out-of-range flow values (531 single-basin models) vs 10 (one 531-basin regional model)

tier3_unverified.claim: The authors report a systematic NEGATIVE result on hybrid/physics-informed deep models: 'so far, to our knowledge, all attempts to add physics to (properly trained) streamflow LSTM models in hydrology have produced lower-performing models.' They further argue that apparent gains from architectural or physics-based adaptations in the literature are artifacts of weak baselines - 'it is trivial (but most likely uninteresting) to beat improperly trained models' - noting that of the top 50 hydrology-ML papers per year for 2021-2023 (150 papers surveyed), 122 trained on individual catchments and only 28 on multiple catchments. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION: published claims that hybrid/differentiable hydrologic models beat baselines should be checked for whether the baseline was single-basin-trained; and our project should NOT expect a physics-informed deep architecture to recover the between-site term. CAVEAT: this is an opinion-paper assertion supported by citation, not by a new controlled experiment in this paper, and it concerns streamflow only.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative claim ('all attempts...have produced lower-performing models'); survey counts 122/150 vs 28/150
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (literature survey of 150 papers; 122 single-catchment, 28 multi-catchment, 4 of the 28 co-authored by these authors)

tier3_unverified.claim: Pandit et al. (2025) trained an LSTM on daily nitrate CONCENTRATION at 148 sites across the conterminous US (grab samples + high-frequency sensors, 1980-2022), and report a large collapse from temporal to spatial validation: median KGE = 0.60 under temporal (hold-out-time-at-known-sites) validation versus median KGE = 0.18 under spatial validation for unmonitored basins. This is a ~70% loss of skill purely from moving to ungauged sites, and it is the single most decisive number for our question: a continental-scale deep model with 148 training basins still performs near-worthless (KGE 0.18; KGE=0 is roughly the skill of predicting the mean) at ungauged locations for nitrate concentration.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 temporal vs 0.18 spatial (ungauged); ~0.42 KGE degradation
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: BOTH reported separately and explicitly distinguished by the authors: temporal-holdout (KGE 0.60) and spatial-holdout / ungauged-basin (KGE 0.18). The exact spatial fold construction (k-fold leave-basins-out vs leave-region-out, and whether nested/overlapping basins were grouped as our LOFO does) could NOT be determined from accessible metadata — treat the spatial number as 'spatial-holdout, fold construction unknown'.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 148 sites CONUS

tier3_unverified.claim: Restricting the spatially-validated LSTM to the Mississippi River Basin raised median spatial-holdout KGE only from 0.18 to 0.34 — i.e. even after narrowing to the hydroclimatic region where training data are densest and most relevant (the ag Midwest), ungauged nitrate concentration prediction remained weak. The authors frame spatial validation as a tool for 'quantifying the impact of current data gaps' and use it to RESTRICT where the model is allowed to be applied, rather than claiming ungauged deployment works. This is a direct precedent for scoping/gating our own deployment map rather than serving predictions at any arbitrary Iowa pin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.18 (CONUS) -> 0.34 (MRB subset); still far below the 0.60 temporal benchmark
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (ungauged-basin), evaluated on the MRB subset
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 148 trained; MRB-applicable subset count not determinable from accessible sources

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE / ABSENCE RESULT for the research angle: no head-to-head comparison of the LSTM against random forest, XGBoost, or any gradient-boosted tree could be found in this paper's abstract, the EPA Science Inventory record for the companion CONUS model, or indexed snippets. The EPA record markets it as 'the first continental-scale LSTM model of nitrate' and, per that record, 'does not reference benchmark comparisons against other machine learning or traditional hydrologic models.' Therefore this paper provides NO evidence that LSTM beats GBDT for ungauged water-quality prediction. It should not be cited to justify replacing our XGBoost with an LSTM. (Caveat: full text was paywalled; a supplementary benchmark table cannot be ruled out.)
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no LSTM-vs-GBDT effect size reported

tier3_unverified.claim: Shapley-value interpretation of the CONUS nitrate LSTM identified TILE DRAINAGE, ROADWAY DENSITY, and WETLAND COVER as the dominant SPATIAL (static, between-site) drivers of mean nitrate concentration, and reported threshold behavior — points beyond which these features exert considerable influence on river chemistry. Catchment attributes were drawn from CAMELS and GAGES-II. This independently corroborates our project's diagnosis that the residual deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE STATIC information: the top three drivers of the site-level mean are all static landscape attributes, and all three (tile drainage, road density, wetland cover) are ABSENT from our current 68-feature set. Falsifiable prediction for us: adding basin-mean tile-drainage fraction, wetland fraction, and road density should improve between_r2 / between_rate_r2 specifically, not within_r2.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative ranking (top spatial drivers) plus unreported threshold values; no per-feature effect size recoverable from accessible sources
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown (interpretation run on the fitted model; not a performance number)

tier3_unverified.claim: OPERATIONAL DATASET, directly closing our known tile-drainage gap: AgTile-US is a 30-m binary raster of modeled tile-drained cropland covering the ENTIRE conterminous US (so it covers all of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of our largest multi-state basins, which is exactly where our current inner-join under-counting is worst). Built from the USDA 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile-drainage statistics, NLCD 2016 cropland, SSURGO soil drainage class, and SRTM slope. Validated against 16,000 ground-truth points at 86.03% CONUS accuracy, and 82.7-93.6% accuracy over the heavily tile-drained Midwest. Static (single epoch, ~2017), GeoTIFF and NetCDF, free public download from Figshare, no authentication. Aggregating this to our existing distance buckets is a small, cheap change and is the only identified source for the control our project flagged as dominant-but-missing.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 86.03% classification accuracy CONUS-wide; 82.7-93.6% in the Midwest, vs 16,000 ground-truth points
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (16,000 validation points)

tier3_unverified.claim: Over 1980-2022 the MRB exported only 19 +/- 4% of nitrogen surplus as riverine nitrate, but Iowa showed extreme wet/dry-year contrast: wet-year export fraction 42 +/- 24% versus dry-year 6 +/- 6% — a ~7x swing attributed to hydrologic connectivity and legacy nitrogen remobilization. Implication for us: the mapping from N-surplus (a static-ish input we already carry, though ours dies in 2017) to realized in-stream nitrate is strongly WETNESS-REGIME DEPENDENT at ANNUAL scale, not daily scale. Our seven failed temporal ablations were all daily/short-window (same-day, lagged, 3D/7D rolling, travel-time-routed). The untested alternative this supports is an ANNUAL or seasonal basin wetness aggregate (e.g. water-year cumulative precipitation percentile) interacted with N-surplus, which is a per-site-year term rather than a daily one — and, crucially, is computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from weather alone. The very large error bars (+/-24 and +/-6) mean this is a noisy relationship and the claim is that direction of effect is real, not that it is precisely estimable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: MRB export 19 +/- 4% of surplus; Iowa wet-year 42 +/- 24% vs dry-year 6 +/- 6% (~7x)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable (descriptive mass-balance result from model application, not a held-out performance number)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: MRB-wide aggregate; contributing basin count not determinable from accessible sources

tier3_unverified.claim: Zhi et al. (2021) trained an LSTM to predict daily river dissolved oxygen from hydrometeorology alone using CAMELS-chem, and on a 'core evaluation group of 84 sites' reported mean (median) NSE, RMSE, and Pearson correlation of 0.51 (0.57), 1.2 (1.1) mg/L, and 0.78 (0.82), with NSE >= 0.4 at 74% of sites. The split protocol behind these numbers is NOT stated in the abstract or the authors' README and the full text is paywalled, so these numbers are NOT comparable to a spatially held-out LOFO benchmark without further verification.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: mean NSE 0.51, median NSE 0.57; RMSE mean 1.2 / median 1.1 mg/L; Pcorr mean 0.78 / median 0.82; 74% of sites NSE >= 0.4
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 236 watersheds in the dataset; 84 sites in the core evaluation group

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE / HIGH-RELEVANCE RESULT: the paper's abstract states plainly 'Surprisingly, the model does not perform better where more data are available.' The authors quantify this as essentially zero relationship between per-site model skill and the number of observations at that site (R2 = 0.03), versus a strong relationship between skill and the site's DO standard deviation (R2 = 0.52). Per-site skill is therefore governed by the character of the site, not by how much training data that site contributes — directly analogous to the sustag finding that headroom is in the between-site term rather than in more site-days.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: skill vs number of data points R2 = 0.03; skill vs DO standard deviation R2 = 0.52
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 84 evaluation sites (of 236)

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper claims LSTM skill is predicted by static/hydroclimatic basin character, specifically that the model 'performs better in basins with low variations of streamflow and DO, high runoff-ratio (>0.45), and winter precipitation peaks.' This is a falsifiable, transferable prediction: a deep model trained on hydrometeorology will systematically underperform in flashy, high-variance, summer-precipitation-dominated agricultural catchments — which describes tile-drained Iowa nitrate basins. It implies the deep-learning advantage reported here would NOT be expected to reproduce in the sustag setting.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative stratification; runoff-ratio threshold quoted as >0.45
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 84 evaluation sites (of 236)

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE TARGET MECHANISM: the abstract states 'The model however misses some DO peaks and troughs when in-stream biogeochemical processes become important.' A hydrometeorology-only deep model captured the physically-forced component (DO solubility vs water temperature) but failed on the biogeochemically-forced extremes. Since the sustag primary target is a threshold-exceedance (violation >= 10 mg/L nitrate), i.e. explicitly an extreme/peak-detection problem under biogeochemical control, this is evidence that switching architecture from XGBoost to LSTM would not address the failure mode that matters here.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative; no quantified peak/trough error reported in accessible material
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 236 watersheds

tier3_unverified.claim: This paper does NOT contain a head-to-head comparison of LSTM against random forest, gradient-boosted trees, or XGBoost. No tree-ensemble baseline appears in the abstract, the authors' repository README, or the citing review's description. It therefore provides ZERO evidence for the research question 'do deep models beat GBDTs for ungauged water-quality prediction' — it establishes only that an LSTM reaches a given absolute skill level, not that it exceeds a boosted-tree alternative.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no baseline comparison identified in any accessible source
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 236 watersheds

tier3_unverified.claim: SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT FLAG: every number in this study rests on 236 watersheds (drawn from a 493-catchment CAMELS-chem pool spanning 1980-2014), and a citing review (Nature npj/PMC11151732) describes a related Zhi et al. ungauged-DO experiment trained on 480 rivers to predict 100 'chemically ungauged basins' — attribution of the 480/100 figure to this specific 2021 paper versus a later Zhi et al. paper could NOT be confirmed. Either way, the evidence base is 236-480 training basins versus sustag's 19 independent basin families, a 12-25x gap. The paper's own finding that skill does not scale with per-site data volume means the deep model's leverage comes from the BREADTH of the basin sample, exactly the resource sustag lacks; an LSTM at n=19 families should not be expected to reproduce these results.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 236 basins (this paper) vs 19 independent basin families in sustag = ~12x; 480 basins in the possibly-related PUB experiment = ~25x
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 236 (this paper); 493 in the parent CAMELS-chem dataset; 480 train / 100 held-out in a related-but-unconfirmed experiment

tier3_unverified.claim: In the study's ungauged-basin (PUB) experiment, a single top-down LSTM trained on all 782 monitored sites ("LSTM conus") beat both regionally-grouped LSTMs and a bottom-up transfer-learning approach at 580 site-disjoint held-out sites: median per-site RMSE 1.43C (+/-0.98) for LSTM conus vs 1.98C (+/-1.78) for LSTM regional (grouped by the 18 HUC-2 regions), 2.02C (+/-1.66) for LSTM cluster (grouped by catchment-attribute similarity), and 2.00C (+/-1.07) for the MTL bottom-up donor-transfer method. Sites achieving RMSE < 2C: 406/580 (LSTM conus) vs 293 / 287 / 290. LSTM conus had the lowest median RMSE in 14 of 17 regions and 14 of 15 attribute clusters. CAVEAT ON PROTOCOL: the train/test split was made by RECORD LENGTH, not geography — the 782 sites with >=5 years of data trained, the 580 sites with 1-5 years tested. It is genuinely site-disjoint (no test site's own observations are seen), but test sites are geographically INTERSPERSED with training sites and there is no region-level separation and no control for nested/overlapping basins. This is therefore a WEAKER spatial holdout than the project's leave-one-basin-family-out LOFO, and 1.43C is NOT directly comparable to our LOFO numbers.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median per-site RMSE 1.43C vs 1.98C / 2.02C / 2.00C; 406 vs 293/287/290 sites under 2C RMSE
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint held-out sites, but split assigned by record length, not by region or basin nesting)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1362 total sites (782 train / 580 test); Experiment 2 extended set 2999 sites (1346 train)

tier3_unverified.claim: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT — this paper contains an explicit demonstration that deep models trained on small numbers of basins collapse at ungauged sites. The authors state: "the grouped models do quite poorly in all regions with less than 15 training sites" and "When only a few sites are available for training... the models are not seeing sufficient data and site diversity in these cases to be able to extrapolate to unseen locations." Worst cases: Lower Colorado (HUC 15) with only 2 training sites — regional LSTM median RMSE 6.38C vs 2.10C for the CONUS model trained on all 782 sites (3.0x worse); Souris-Red-Rainy (HUC 09) — regional LSTM 9.09C and cluster LSTM 8.70C, versus a CONUS-model worst-region value of 2.34C (California, HUC 18). Region sizes where grouped models worked were much larger (e.g. Pacific Northwest, 142 training sites, regional LSTM 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C). IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our 19 independent basin families sits well below the ~15-site threshold at which this paper observed catastrophic grouped-model failure, and far below the 142-site region where a regional deep model was competitive. The LSTM advantage documented here is an effect of LARGE-SAMPLE SITE DIVERSITY (782-1346 basins), not of the architecture per se, and there is no evidence in this paper that it survives at n~19.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Lower Colorado (2 train sites): regional LSTM 6.38C vs CONUS 2.10C. Souris-Red-Rainy: regional 9.09C, cluster 8.70C. Pacific Northwest (142 train sites): regional 1.27C vs CONUS 1.22C
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint; regional models trained on a region's sites and tested on other held-out sites within that same region)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: regional models trained on per-HUC subsets of 782 sites; failing regions had 2-15 training sites, succeeding regions had 47-183

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON TRAINING-SET SIZE — the paper's explicit data-volume ablation found performance SATURATES: expanding the training set from ~3.82 million observations across 782 sites to ~6.13 million observations across 1346 sites produced NO improvement for the meteorology-only and meteorology+lat/long/altitude models, and only marginal improvement for the models that included discharge (median per-site RMSE 1.57C -> 1.50C) or GAGES-II catchment attributes (1.47C -> 1.43C). The authors conclude: "while increasing data volumes can partially offset the absence of certain input types, its effects may be limited beyond a certain training dataset size." This is a two-edged claim for this project: it means the marginal value of adding basins is strongly diminishing ABOVE ~800 basins, but it says nothing about the region below 100 basins, where the grouped-model failures above show the curve is extremely steep. The paper reports no ablation sweeping training-basin count downward, so it CANNOT be used to estimate what performance is achievable at n=19.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no RMSE improvement for meteo-only and meteo+location models; discharge model 1.57C->1.50C; GAGES-II attributes model 1.47C->1.43C
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (site-disjoint held-out sites, split by record length)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 782 -> 1346 training sites (3.82M -> 6.13M observations); 580 test sites

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE 'CHEAPER MIDDLE GROUND' OF REGIONAL FINE-TUNING — the authors tested fine-tuning the large top-down model on data from each target region (the standard remedy for small regional sample sizes, citing Oruche et al. 2021 and Zhu & Zhou 2024) and report that the technique "yielded performance that mirrored the top-down model very closely when applied to both the grouped modeling and bottom-up approaches." That is, region-specific adaptation added essentially nothing over the global model and did not recover the deficit of the small-sample regional models. No numeric table is given for this fine-tuning experiment in the main text, so the effect size is unquantified. This is evidence against expecting gains from region- or site-specific adaptation layers on top of a global model when the local sample is small — relevant to any proposal to layer per-site random effects or site embeddings on top of the existing booster, though it tests fine-tuning specifically, not embeddings or random effects, which this paper does not evaluate at all.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: unquantified in main text — described only as performance that "mirrored the top-down model very closely"
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 782 train / 580 test (regional subsets)

tier3_unverified.claim: STATIC CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES MATTERED MORE THAN DYNAMIC DISCHARGE, AND A SMALL CURATED STATIC SET WAS AS GOOD AS 274 ATTRIBUTES. Starting from a meteorology-only model (median per-site RMSE 1.78C), adding the 274 GAGES-II static catchment attributes dropped RMSE to 1.47C, while adding river discharge instead dropped it only to 1.57C; the full model with both reached 1.43C. Adding location (lat/long/elevation) to meteorology "did not meaningfully improve performance." Combined permutation importance was 3.97C for the three air-temperature inputs, 1.12C for all 274 GAGES-II attributes combined, and only 0.36C for all discharge features combined. In Experiment 3, replacing the 274 attributes with just 21 EXPERT-SELECTED attributes gave statistically equivalent accuracy (median RMSE 1.46C vs 1.43C) and was actually BETTER on the warmest 10% of observations (1.64C vs 1.70C), and was the best of the three attribute sets at 218/580 test sites vs 186/580 for the full 274-attribute default; a 25-attribute aggregated-z-score set gave 1.47C. Most important individual expert-selected attributes: percent slope (PCT_SLOPE, 0.10C) and drainage area (DRAIN_SQKM, 0.08C); in the z-score model the top category was "Major Dams" (0.16C). RELEVANCE: this supports the project's own finding that static between-site geography, not temporal dynamics, carries the transferable signal — and shows ~20 well-chosen static attributes suffice, which is tractable at n=19 in a way that 274 attributes is not.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: meteo-only 1.78C; +discharge 1.57C; +GAGES-II attributes 1.47C; both 1.43C. 21 expert attributes 1.46C vs 274 attributes 1.43C (warmest-10%: 1.64C vs 1.70C). Permutation importance: air temp 3.97C, attributes 1.12C, discharge 0.36C
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 782 train / 580 test

tier3_unverified.claim: THIS PAPER DOES NOT PROVIDE A HEAD-TO-HEAD LSTM-vs-GRADIENT-BOOSTED-TREE COMPARISON ON THE PREDICTION TASK, AND CONTAINS NO NITRATE OR NUTRIENT-CONCENTRATION RESULT AT ALL. XGBoost appears only as a META-model inside the bottom-up MTL pipeline — it predicts the expected RMSE of transferring a single-site LSTM to a target site (152 estimators, learning rate 0.183, 234 features after RFECV), and is used to select the 10 best donor sites; it never predicts stream temperature directly. The only XGBoost-vs-LSTM accuracy figures in the paper are a CROSS-PAPER, CROSS-PROTOCOL comparison the authors themselves flag as non-equivalent: Weierbach et al. (2022) reported MONTHLY stream-temperature RMSE of 0.61C for XGBoost, 0.89C for support vector regression and 1.2C for multilinear regression in the Pacific Northwest (n=54 total sites) and mid-Atlantic (n=24 total sites) using a random-subsampling 100-member ensemble, versus LSTM conus DAILY median RMSE of 1.22C (Pacific Northwest, 208 total / 70 test sites) and 1.27C (mid-Atlantic, 212 total / 121 test sites). These numbers CANNOT be compared — different temporal aggregation (monthly vs daily) and different split protocol (random subsampling vs record-length site holdout). Conclusion for the research angle: this source supplies NO evidence that LSTMs beat XGBoost for ungauged-basin water-quality prediction; its contribution is evidence that TRAINING-SET BREADTH (number and diversity of basins), not architecture, is what drives ungauged-basin skill.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: XGBoost 0.61C monthly RMSE (Weierbach 2022) vs LSTM conus 1.22C/1.27C daily RMSE — explicitly non-comparable per the authors
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: mixed and non-comparable — Weierbach 2022 used random subsampling over a 100-member ensemble; this paper used record-length site-disjoint holdout
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Weierbach 2022: n=54 (Pacific Northwest) and n=24 (mid-Atlantic) total sites. This paper's corresponding regions: 208 total/70 test and 212 total/121 test
